utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is still continuing with examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, before you do --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to my learned colleague, but it looks like we have some technical difficulties. One of these earphones are not working well. So if someone from the technical staff could assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we'll get some assistance from the technical people. It's all right now? Okay. All right. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I just have, upon reflection, one sort of explanation, clarification, if you like, that you might seek from the witness. Yesterday we were told that at a certain point in time in Bosanski Samac that the witness in order to -- to walk was sort of bent over, and the witness demonstrated her problem and so on. I'd just like to find out what was the reason for the deterioration in her back, her legs that made this happen, in terms of her general health condition and specifically what she showed and demonstrated to us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Weiner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Drljacic. Judge Williams just asked a question. She said yesterday you were discussing your physical condition, how poor your back had become. And she wanted to know what caused that poor physical condition in your back, in your body that made you walk in this bent over state with a cane or a stick or something. Could you please explain it to the Judge.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. I hadn't been in very good health before either, but the conditions of living had made my condition deteriorate. For two winters I didn't have a bath in warm water. It was sciatica which prevented me from standing up straight or lying down or sitting down without feeling pain. I didn't have hot water because we didn't have electricity. We hadn't been prepared for that, and we hadn't got hold of a stove which uses firewood, and I had nowhere to store the firewood anyway. So I had to make do with what we had, just as everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to check with all the Defence counsel. Can everyone -- okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday, ma'am, we left off -- yesterday we left off, and you were telling us how you had been evicted from your apartment by two police officers. They ordered you to unlock the door and they took your keys. Did they tell you to pack your bags or to take your things at that point? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew what it was all about as soon as they took the keys, and I asked them if I could take one travel bag which I had already prepared. Although I hadn't thought I would be evicted, because I didn't have a son or husband who could have either crossed the river or resist by refusing to accept a rifle. My only family remaining in town was that brother. He was the closest person I had. Those two soldiers, or rather, policemen allowed me to take this travel bag, which I was unable to carry down. And the two of them carried it for me downstairs, and I took with me some sort of trolly in order to be able to take the travel bag to my brother's home. And we had agreed, as I said yesterday, that if my brother came back from his work obligation in time would go there at 7.00 -- or before 7.00 to pick up the sewing machine, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when those two police officers evicted you from your apartment, did they tell you who was going to be moving into your apartment after you left that evening?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask, nor did they tell me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone move into your apartment after you were evicted?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't the faintest. I don't know. I didn't dare to ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall speaking with some investigators from the Tribunal, ma'am, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Salt Lake City.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall -- do you recall them -- and just see if this refreshes your recollection -- telling you that -- telling the investigator that is the police officers told you that you had to leave because they wanted to settle a Serb family in your apartment? Does that refresh your recollection, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a common occurrence which I didn't even pay much attention to. At the time I was still in a state of shock, and it was normal that as soon as I moved out they would move somebody else in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you still remained in Bosanski Samac after you got evicted for a few months. During that time, during those few months, two, three months, did you learn that anyone had moved into your apartment?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I didn't pass by and couldn't see, and I had no one to ask. There was nobody there whom I could have asked. All the people living there were Serbs, and they wouldn't tell me nor would I have dared to ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take that answer, ma'am. What happened to your Muslim and Croatian neighbours that were living in your building?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my stairwell, I'm the only Muslim woman. Bahrija was in some sort of mixed marriage. Although, earlier I never thought about who was Catholic, who was Orthodox, and who was Muslim. That -- that's not the way I was brought up, and I was really amazed how it could have come about that one nation or one confession is suddenly elevated above the others. Until then people entered into mixed marriages, had children. I have two nieces. My sister married a man who was not a Muslim, and he too came from a mixed marriage. His mother was Muslim, and his father was a Hungarian. So who are the children, then? I never thought anything like that would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Why don't we try again. What happened to any of the non-Serbian neighbours living in your building or the building next door? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same building but in a different entranceway all vacant apartments were immediately taken over by people of Orthodox, Christian faith who had abandoned smaller apartments to move into larger ones or they had had no apartments of their own before. In any case, they immediately occupied those vacant apartments in the -- in a different entranceway. And in my entranceway, on the fourth floor four Croats resided. Mladjo remained -- stayed behind after I left, whereas two out of the other three apartments were occupied by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Two questions based on what you just said. First, you indicated that there were vacant apartments that were immediately taken over by Orthodox Christians. Where did these Orthodox Christians or Serbs come from? Were they local people, or did they come from out of town?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time there were only local people or alternatively people from the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they moved into vacant apartments. What happened to the people that lived in those apartments?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you what happened to them individually. In any case, from that other entranceway I know the only man who remained -- I don't remember the name. It was a Muslim man. As for the other men, at the beginning families were not taken into custody or taken away. But after some man had crossed the river, the families were taken away too. I had already mentioned Ruza the Italian, whose son was among the five men who first came into my entranceway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who what did Ruza do?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ruza moved into a two-room apartment. I'm not sure whether it had two or three rooms, but it was previously owned by a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were talking about vacancies. What happened in 1992 and 1993 to the vacant apartments in Bosanski Samac? What was happening to these vacant apartments?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first they were looted, unless somebody was settled in them -- both apartments and houses. If somebody had already moved in, they lived there for a while -- maybe until the end. But if those settlers moved on, they would take with them all the things from that apartment or in certain cases those people moved in into apartments which had already been looted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say these apartments were looted, tell the Court what type of things were taken from these apartments.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything. Furniture, even clothes, everything. They left only the bare walls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I presume we're going to find out how the witness knows this, being that she never returned to her own apartment to see what had happened there. If you could perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how soon did this looting or these takings occur? Assuming that the war started in April of 1992, how soon after the war started did these lootings or takings of property from vacant apartments occur?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the -- the apartments were evacuated, both apartments and houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you ever see anyone taking materials or property, or did you ever see people carrying off or vehicles with property? Tell the Court what you saw.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not uncommon for people to come on a truck, pick up all the property from a house and put it on a truck. When my neighbour -- when my brother Hamza's house was looted, I was an eyewitness. When the things were carried away, my brother tried to save my sewing machine, but he got a beating. Of course it was the Orthodox people who did this. They had all the rights, and we had no right even to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said the Orthodox people were the ones who were doing this or looting. Of what ethnic group were the Orthodox people?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: They call themselves Serbs, and I don't dispute that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people whose apartments were being looted or whose property were being -- was being taken, of what ethnic group were they?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Serbs? Were any Serb homes being looted and property being taken from them?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. On the contrary. The looted things were carried into their apartments or the apartments which they intended to occupy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you saw the people doing this, were these people in uniform? Were these locals? Were these civilians? Tell us about who was doing this?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was mostly local people or people from the surrounding villages, at the beginning. Later, after I had left, I heard that Serb refugees had started to arrive, and I don't know what happened later but I heard that those people were forced to move into empty houses, which were in certain cases damaged or demolished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you need a glass of water, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said later after you left. Are you talking about 1994 that you heard this was happening?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right [Interpretation] That's right. When we were able to contact the people who remained in Samac throughout, we learned about the Serb refugees and what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, before you do, again just as a matter of clarification here. I wonder whether the witness could tell us how she knows that property that was taken from apartments or homes owned by non-Serbs, how she knows that this property was later, according to page 7, line 19: "these looted things were carried into there," i.e., from the text here -- the context "Serb apartments or the apartments they intended to occupy." Maybe the witness could tell us how she knows that the property went from non-Serb apartments into Serb apartments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear the Judge's question, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an eyewitness to that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no need to apologise. You saw some of this. Did any of your neighbours or colleagues during 1992 or 1993 -- did any of your Muslim or Croatian neighbours or colleagues see this same thing happening?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us were eyewitnesses to that, including, I believe, the accused here present. I not only believe that, I am certain that they saw this with their own eyes as well as I did, and I mean the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you say that, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that just because it -- it should grate on their ears too. Time has come for the truth to be told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- let me -- let me ask you a few questions on that. When these things were happening, these -- the property being looted from apartments, you said trucks were being used. So people were carrying furniture out on trucks. Was this being done in the wide open daylight or in the secret of the night?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in broad daylight. Nobody was trying to hide anything from anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this happening all over town or just on your street?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: All over town. Even in villages. Women from Samac would go around villages, loot, and bring the looted things back to Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see them carrying these looted goods back into Samac?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't hide anything. Nothing was hidden. A concrete example: A neighbour of mine that lived in the yard next door -- I was very surprised about this. She had a rope attached from the cinema to her window. And one day she would only wash curtains and she would dry them on these ropes. The next day she would only wash, say, knitted sweaters or other kinds of handiwork, doilies. And these doilies were made with a lot of effort by others, because she never had them before. This didn't happen once. This was going on day after day after day that she would wash curtains one day, then this handiwork the next, and these doilies. This handiwork was very valuable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understand your answer correctly, she didn't have this property prior to the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: She couldn't have these huge quantities. She could have had as much as I made for myself. But she couldn't have had two or three whole lines of these objects, and this was happening on more than one occasion. This didn't happen just on one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about houses being looted. What about shops or stores? Were they looted in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stores were looted on the same day. They were emptied; I don't know how. My brother was in a store. He worked at the ironworks. And he came to work in the morning. But those areas where people didn't work, everything was taken out of those. For example, out of the department store, which was closed. I don't know who took all the goods out of these stores though. For example, certain machines from factories were taken out, and they were driven to Serbia. I also know that cattle was loaded on trucks, and it was taken to Serbia. All the more valuable things were taken to Serbia, and that is how many people in Serbia got rich. And those people weren't rich before. None of us was really rich before. But today people who had nothing have a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a follow-up question, ma'am: How do you know these things were taken to Serbia? You said these things were loaded on trucks. So there was cattle or machinery from the factories. How do you know it went to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. Everybody else knows; even those present here, the accused. It might even be the case that one of them drove those goods to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you ever see the license plates on these trucks that were leaving town with the goods?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never paid attention to the license plates. They also took our cars. So they could have changed the license plates and used whichever ones they wanted. But I never paid attention to license plates. All cars belonging to Croats and Muslims were taken away, allegedly because they were needed for military purposes. But people recognised their cars, and they also recognised the people driving their own cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that in a few minutes. But let's stay on with the looting. Who did the work? Who did the removal of all of these -- all of these pieces of machinery and the cattle? Who did the work of actually transporting this, carrying it? Who did that work?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very frequently this was done by the Muslims who were -- who had to carry out work -- forced labour for a Serb. A lot of people -- a lot of -- very often people that were under a work obligation, they were told this was a work obligation but this was forced labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these people who did the work, did you ever speak to them about what type of work they were doing, these Muslims and Croats that were doing this work, carrying these items out, the machinery and the cattle? Did you speak to them during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. The Muslims and Croats that were doing this forced labour, did you get a chance to speak to them and talk to them about the work they were doing? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have to ask. Everybody talked what was happening to their nearest and dearest. And then people would spread this information, so we knew what was going on. This was not a secret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not asking if it was a secret. Did you speak to people who were doing some of this work? Did you speak to any of please Muslims or Croats that were doing some of this work?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. As I said, they all worked. Everybody did something, and they all talked about what they had to do. I can't -- it's hard to say specifically who did what, but everybody did whatever they were ordered, whatever was necessary. They had no opportunity to choose what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just talk generally for a moment. The people who were carrying these goods out, the people who told you how they were carrying pieces of machinery out, putting it on trucks, bringing cattle out, putting that on trucks, did they tell you that it was being transported to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can say specifically, for example, people from Samac had to load on the orders from Odzak things like furniture for the bedroom or the living room, and I was an eyewitness. When Pancir's mother asked to have from Odzak taken for her brother something that was looted from a Muslim, her brother, however, was a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- he was allegedly a member. He was not a detainee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were present when Pancir's mother --

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was detained in Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were present when Pancir's mother made the request some good to be looted from a Muslim home in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was there when she was yelling after the people who were on the truck. She said, "Bring me this and that for my Jovo." He is detained. He's in a camp. He's being -- he's detained by the Muslims. But as I said, he was actually a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Pancir's mother, are you referring to Mile Pancir, Mile, nicknamed Pancir?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I didn't remind you that this was Mile Pancir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of what ethnic group did she belong to?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, we talked a few minutes ago about shops being looted. Did you have a brother whose nickname was Hamza?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the war broke out, he was in the shop. And then the next time he came to work, he worked for another month, a month and a half until he was moved out of there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's -- I want to ask you a few other questions about him, not about his employment. Did he have a home -- actually, what was his name? We know his nickname was Hamza. What was his full name?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Salih Drljacic, but everybody knows him as Hamza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you brother own a home that had a grocery store on the first floor that he was renting out? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had a house and on the first floor there was a store that he was renting out. And this store was open until that night, and then it was closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This store that he had, who did he rent it out to?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He rented it out to a man who owned several stores in Samac. He also had a store in the part of the house that belonged to Miro Brko. Whether he was the owner of that store or he just rented it out, I don't know, but the store was either in Miro Brko's home -- house or in the house right next to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say he had a store, what kind of store are we talking about? Is this a grocery store? Is this a hardware store, a furniture store? What type of store did he have in your brother's home?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two stores that I mentioned were grocery stores.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and of what ethnic group did the man who was renting out the grocery store from your brother belong to? Just what ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Croat. He was killed in the first days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What happened to his store that was located in your brother's house in April of 1992? What happened to that store in that -- during that month? And we're talking about the time after the war started.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The store that was located in my brother's house -- this is what happened: The Serbs came, made a list what was located in the store at that moment, and then they took everything away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your brother or anyone else give them permission to take these goods in the grocery store?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't even asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they made a list. Did they leave a receipt or leave a note for the owner -- or for your brother?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. They left absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said your brother worked in another shop, your brother, Hamza, who owned this store. He worked at a different store; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He worked at the company called Jeljezara, the ironworks, and he rented this store in his house. His son's wife worked in that store.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's talk about your brother's job just for a few minutes. Did he hold a position in the shop that he worked, at the ironworks? Was he a manager? Was he a director?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother worked for Bosanka for 44 years. In this store he worked several years as a manager.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was a manager of the Bosanka store? Is that how you pronounce it?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the manager of the store.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what did they sell at that shop or that store?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were selling agricultural equipment, smaller machines for agricultural needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did something happen to his job in June of 1992? Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was replaced. He was replaced by Nada Vukovic. She was the sister of the person whom we called Majmun, last name also Vukovic. Before my brother was fired, his daughter and two children whose husband swam across the river and Hamza's wife, Sevla, they were all rounded up and taken to the camp. He remained for another month, month and a half, and he was working. But when he was fired, he was also taken to the camp, where his wife and children were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was he fired after 40 or more years? Was it 44 years working there and he was a manager. Why did they fire him?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Muslim, and he wasn't allowed to work. He wasn't allowed to work for salary. He was being paid while he worked there, but he wasn't allowed to do so any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person who replaced him -- the woman who replaced him, of what ethnic group did he belong, Nada Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was an Orthodox Christian from Croatia, just like her brother Vukovic. They were from some village in Croatia, somewhere around Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were any other Muslims or Croats fired from their jobs after the war began in 1992, in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody was allowed to work for salary ever again. They had to leave all their jobs, all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they" or "nobody," people of what ethnic group are you referring to were fired from their jobs or were not going to be paid any more?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "nobody," I'm referring to Muslims or Croats. When I say "they," this refers to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said "they had to leave all their jobs, all of them." The Serbs had to leave their jobs or the Muslims or Croats had to leave --

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims. Muslims and Croats had to leave their jobs. I apologise. I got a little bit confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing to apologise about. Don't worry. All right. We were talking about property that was being taken from Muslims and Croats, and you mentioned vehicles were taken. Can you -- you started to talk about that before. Could you tell the Court what happened to the vehicles that were owned by the Muslims and Croats in April of 1992 after the war began.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: All cars belonging to Muslims and Croats were immediately taken away from them, allegedly because of military needs. But people saw others driving their cars privately, in their private lives. Serbs were driving Muslim and Croat cars, cars belonging to Muslims and Croats, in their everyday lives, even though these cars were requisitioned because of military needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the cars owned by Serbs, the Serb citizens of Bosanski Samac? Were their vehicles taken or requisitioned?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. They kept their cars, and they also got whichever car they wanted that belonged to a Croat or a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's continue on with the services in Bosanski Samac during the summer of 1992. Was there still a local Red Cross? You mentioned earlier that the local Red Cross gave bread and milk out the first two weeks after the war started. During the summer of 1992, was there still a local Red Cross in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, it was -- it was functioning. I believe there is still a Red Cross. And we were getting things for free. I also tried to go to the Red Cross and get help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask you. In the summer of 1992, middle part of the summer, did you hear that the Red Cross had received some goods, some food?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever go to the Red Cross and ask for some?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the Red Cross was distributing food at the old hotel. The son of Cviko Bosic was the one distributing it. I heard from many Muslims that they received food, and that is why I also went there, to try to get some myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell -- and when you went there, did you see Cviko Bozic's son, when you went to the local Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went into his office, and he asked me what I wanted. I said I also came to get some food, to get a parcel. That's what I said. That's how we called it. We called it "parcels." And he said, "There is nothing here. Alija has some. Why don't you go there?" And I had no further comment. I went out, and I never went back to ask for more food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he said, "Alija has some. Why don't you go there," who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The then-president of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continuing on with services in Bosanski Samac, let's move into late 1992, early 1993. Did you ever have to see a doctor? You talked about the problem you were having with your back. In early 1993, did you ever go see a doctor in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to. My condition was such that I needed medical help. The doctor received me. He talked to me. And then he said, "Unfortunately we have no medication. We can't help you," although I knew that there had been some donations received and certain doctors gave medicines out without a prescription and without any payments. I, however, didn't get any medication from this doctor, even though there were medications available from donations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there were medications available and some doctors did give them out. I assume gave them out to Muslims and Croats. Did any doctor ever give you any medication at about that same time?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the health centre, nobody gave me any medication. However, Dr. Sisic must have seen me on the street, and he asked my brother furtively not -- and he asked my brother not to tell anyone. He sent me two packets of pills. I don't know what they were for, but I took them anyway. But they didn't help. Maybe I needed something else. He tried to help me, and I -- for that, I will be forever grateful. There were very few honest people, and he was one of them. He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you all right to continue, ma'am? Are you okay? All right. Let's go on a little bit more. How many houses of worship were there in Bosanski Samac in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an Orthodox church, a Catholic church, and one mosque, so three places of worship altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you previously talked about the mosque, and you indicated that it was blown up apparently in the summer of 1992. You mentioned that yesterday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was a very strong explosion. Pieces that were -- belonged to the base ended up on the roof of the department store. Also, a lot of glass was broken, and the roofs from the neighbouring houses were also damaged, and tiles on the roofs of surrounding houses were also quite damaged from the explosion, so that a lot of people had to do work on their houses after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the mosque completely destroyed after that explosion?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely. Some other Muslims, including myself, tried to use some remains of the wood -- some of the wood that remained from the church, so we could use this for firewood. To my great surprise, grass has appeared very quickly on that location, and I was wondering how this could be because there -- a building had been on this location for such a long time and how could grass grow on a place that was dead for so long, because a house was upon it, a mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was also a Catholic church in Bosanski Samac. At the end of 1992 -- in a period from the end of 1992 to early 1993, did something happen to the Catholic church in Bosanski Samac? Tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was dismantled manually, piece by piece, because between the Catholic church and the Orthodox church, there was just a short distance. They were across the street from each other. The Orthodox church was in the immediate vicinity therefore, and in order not to damage it they took months to dismantle the Catholic church manually. I was an eyewitness to that. I passed along that street while this was going on. I passed by it two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those times that you passed by, what did you see? How did it look? Was it changing each time over those two months?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Less and less remained of it. However, people continued to come there and take away pieces of wood to use as firewood. Only Muslims and Croats, of course. And we were allowed to do that. Orthodox people were well supplied with firewood because they felled Croat forests. They cut down and cleared Croat forests all the time. And all we had were leftovers, leftovers of firewood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the people who were taking the firewood, who was doing the work dismantling the Catholic church at the end of 1992 and in early 1993? Who was doing that work dismantling that church?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: All menial tasks were done exclusively by Muslims, and I believe they dismantled the Catholic church too, on the orders of Serbs of course. Since it was a time-consuming job, they didn't want to do it themselves. Maybe they had a hand in it too, but I think it was mainly the Muslims who did the dismantling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you believe it was the Muslims who did the dismantling, are you talking about the people who were on forced labour?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. People who were doing forced labour, I believe this was them who dismantled the Catholic church. They may have even filmed the process to have Muslims on tape doing this job and later spread stories that it was the Muslims who did it. Later a teacher from Serbia came and said, "I can understand that Croats escaped by crossing the river, but I don't understand how they took dynamite with them in order to blow up the mosque. You see how well they were prepared."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's just take it one step at a time. So we talked about the Muslims on forced labour were the persons who dismantled the church. Did they do this voluntarily, or were they ordered to do this?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who would do it voluntarily? Is there anyone who would do forced labour voluntarily? I don't know such a person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversations with persons doing forced labour who told you about having to dismantle the church?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you the names of people who worked on the church. I know that it was done by Muslims on somebody's orders; I don't know whose. The accused are better placed to know who issued those words, and I suppose they too destroyed the church. Because it was hard work. You had to crack the concrete blocks piece by piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I wonder whether we could find out from the witness -- she mentions on page 21, line 21 that they -- and I believe she's meaning Serbian people -- they may have even filmed the process to have Muslims on tape doing this job, i.e., the dismantling of the Catholic church. I'm just wondering whether the witness heard that in fact there was a film made or whether this is just a speculation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you heard the Judge's question. I know previously, yesterday you spoke about filming the people in the lines getting food and milk, and it was shown on television Belgrade. Was something similar done? Did you see any filming or cameras or did you hear about it, or is it just some speculation that it might have been done? Please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were any speculations, but I know that they used various footage involving Muslims. I saw on that site many people who had come there to collect wood, and I don't think they belonged to the group of people who did so of their own free will, as I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- let's continue to take that step by step. You said they used various footage including the Muslims. So we need some clarification. I'm not certain about what your answer is. Let's take it slowly. Were you aware of any cameras or photography of the dismantle -- that was occurring during the dismantling of that church?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it with my own eyes, but I heard that footage was made of all the people who performed labour, and I believe -- I suppose that includes people who dismantled the church. I don't think -- I can't believe that the church was an exception to that. They filmed Muslims taking property out of houses, probably to -- to present it in a different light and insinuate that it was the Muslims who looted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "they filmed," who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs did the filming. Muslims did not dare to show that they owned a camera, a still camera or a video camera. People who were once detained did not come back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most case, they were later exchanged, except for those who were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. A few further questions. You talked about people taking firewood, taking wood home from the dismantling site for firewood. And you also said that there were people there who were taking wood for fireplaces but they weren't doing it voluntarily. Were you saying that some people -- some people were doing certain -- some people were ordered to take wood to bring to others as part of a forced labour-type assignment?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not understand me correctly. We who picked up pieces of wood, we did so to use it as firewood. Serbs didn't need to do that, because they were well supplied with firewood. They were given whole trailers full of firewood, and they cut down whole forests. They didn't need to go and collect pieces of wood. That -- that's something that only we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's because you weren't given quantities of wood -- meaning you -- the Muslims and Croats weren't given quantities of wood; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't get anything, and we had not prepared for the situation that eventually occurred. Not a single Muslim had prepared themselves for what happened. We didn't get hold of appropriate stoves which use firewood. We would gather in the rare places where there were working stoves to cook something or to bake bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. One final question: You made a statement earlier while we were talking about the church about some -- about a story that was made up about the mosque that someone -- that people -- one was saying, "How could the Croats try and carry explosives on their back?" Could you explain that again -- "and swim across the river." Were they trying to say that the Croats had blown up the mosque in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the claim of one teacher, a man from Serbia who had worked in Samac for a long time as a teacher, teaching sciences. His name was Kolev, K-o-l-e-v.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just tell the Court again what his claim was.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He claimed that it was the Croats who had blown up the mosque. However, there remained a trace of the fuse, and everybody could see where it led. Everybody could see from where the mosque was blown up. And he was trying to convince everyone that it was the Croats who did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the scene where the mosque had been blown up and disappeared after this occurred?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you. I went to pick up firewood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to see this fuse?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't follow such things. But other Muslims saw it, and I believe they also knew the name of the man who did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I want to know how much more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Not much. Less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the last part of our testimony. Exchanges. Were exchanges occurring in Bosanski Samac during 1992 and 1993, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Bosanski Samac, exchanges took place frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least until I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see people off before they were exchanged, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I followed every exchange that I knew about; however, they -- there were exchanges that I did not know about. Thus, for instance, one year before my brother and I left, his wife and child left. The eldest brother's wife and son who had been brought over from Batkovici left. I didn't know about these exchanges, so I didn't manage to see them off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just talk about the ones that you had seen. Where did you go to see people off, when you said you followed them. Where did you go to see these people off before they were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly point for exchanges was the schoolyard of the primary school and of the secondary school centre, the playground outside, and that was where I came to see off my fellow townsfolk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see any of the defendants there at every one of those exchanges?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miro Brko was there at every exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Miro Brko, are you referring to the accused Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I mean him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there anyone else with him coordinating those exchanges?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. There were the people who organised the exchange. Most often he would be there. Those people who had the opportunity contacted him beforehand. And if they had money to offer him, they would get priority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't care who was left behind

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Let's -- let's go to the people first who were coordinating the exchanges. You said you used to see Miroslav Tadic at these exchanges. Do you know a man by the name of Sveto Vasovic?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We called him Obrvas, meaning "thick eyebrows."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see Sveto Vasovic at these exchanges -- or at these gatherings prior to the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time that I was there he or the Obrvas person would read out their list. And according to that list, people would get on the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the accused Miroslav Tadic ever read out the list when they gathered for these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He read out the lists, and people would get on the bus as their names were called out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you talked about people taking money in Bosanski Samac to have their name placed on the exchange list. Who was taking the money to have their names -- to have -- who was taking the money and placing names on the exchange lists? Who was taking those bribes?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an open secret. Everybody could go and see Miro Brko and grease his palm, or they could go to Obrvas and pay him. I didn't even know about this before I left. If I had known, maybe I would have gone to see them too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Obrvas," you're referring to Sveto Vasovic?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sveto, yes. I'm sorry about this. We always use nicknames in Samac, and I don't always remember to say his name instead of his nickname. But I have already confirmed that this was his nickname. If I say "Obrvas," I mean Sveto Vasovic; and if I say "Miro Brko," it means Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you learned after you were exchanged about people bribing Sveto Vasovic and Miroslav Tadic. Did anyone tell you after they'd been exchanged -- were people telling you that they had paid to get exchanged?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right. People paid money in order to be able to get out. I can tell you specifically. The first people to be taken out by Miro Tadic were Croats, such as the family of the director of Mladost company. He drove his family personally in his own car for 5.000 Deutschmark. Those were the first people who got out. Whereas, we others were unable to leave Samac at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who received the 5.000 Deutschmarks and drove the family of Juro Krajinovic out of Bosanski Samac? Who you said "he." Who was that?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Miro Brko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I used the name Juro Krajinovic. Was Juro Krajinovic the director of the Mladost company? Is he the person you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used to be the director of the finishing process -- finishing and processing at the Mladost company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said the defendant or the accused Miroslav Tadic drove this family out. Did he also drive Juro Krajinovic out of Bosanski Samac at that time?

utterances.speaker: Hajrija Drljacic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Juro Krajinovic was detained together with other Croats. And I don't know whether he left at the same time as his family, but I know for a fact that his family was taken out of Samac by Miro Brko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any members of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that we have already accepted the practice that when the evidence is hearsay, the witness should try to explain in greater detail the source of their information. Now, the question is being asked where she got this information for the first time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer this? From everyone in Zasavica. And Miroslav Tadic knows that the daughter of my sister was married in Zasavica and that Pero and Juro were their other close relatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean all the people in Zasavica told you that the money was being paid to Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Juro told his friends. His friends told all the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we break --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a break now, please. I'm not feeling very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a break and continue at 16.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the break the witness became ill -- or just before the break, while on the stand she had some sort of stress or chest pains. She was brought to the witness room. The nurse was called. Her blood pressure was high. They took her blood pressure a second time, and it had decreased somewhat, but it was the nurse's recommendation that she should not go on. It was victim/witness's recommendation that she should not go on, and she didn't feel well and didn't want to continue. Our plan was to put her on initially probably another 45 minutes today and then cross-examination. As a result, we don't have anyone else lined up to testify today. There are some administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Then we'll continue testimony hopefully on Tuesday at 14.15 hours. We hope that she'll be -- she will have recovered by then. Yes. The Trial Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise some matters regarding witnesses. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm about to do that. But may I just take this opportunity if I can to just present another document. Perhaps it's best if we deal with it now. It's the document referred to the other day by Mr. Esad Dagovic. It should be put under seal, because it's the document that had his address on it, if you recall. He was concerned about that. It was one of the documents that he produced showing his employment in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was briefly discussed. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That can be produced under seal. MR. DI FAZIO: I think it's -- I believe it's to be P60 ter ID -- P60 ter. So if I could just produce the original now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And ask that it be dealt with. Then I'll move on to the main matter that I wanted to raise with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So for that document and all the other ones that came in a group, are yet translated into English. MR. DI FAZIO: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: The translations have been requested and should be with us next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. I wondered -- maybe the Defence counsels wish to look at it, if the usher can show them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So can we just have confirmation of the number, please, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This will replace the photocopy provided and will remain as P60/ter under seal -- thank you -- ID for now. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, essentially what I want to do is to ask for a degree of more flexibility in the manner in which we deal with witnesses. And by that I mean whether they give their evidence in the normal, usual manner and the provisions of 92 -- and whether they give their evidence under the provisions of 92 bis. First of all, I want to reiterate and affirm again that the Prosecution has heard everything that the Chamber says about the use of the provisions of 92 bis and reiterate that we are doing everything we can to utilise the provisions of 92 bis. Indeed as I speak, Ms. Reidy is down in Bosnia taking statements. And Mr. Weiner's turn will come soon to -- to carry out the same exercise. But I -- I am concerned that if we're not given more flexibility in the -- with respect to who gives their evidence under 92 bis and who doesn't, we may come to a bit of a grinding halt. To assist, I've provided the Court with a -- a list of witnesses, which is extracted from that other list that I provided to you when I initially made submissions to you on 92 bis, and a calendar, which is with Ms. Atanasio. And I wonder if copies of the calendar and that list could be given to you. I provided the same to Defence counsel. This is just to assist my submissions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: You can see that this witness, number 1, is Hajrija Drljacic. She's currently giving her evidence. I should also add that this is not an order of witnesses. It's just a grouping of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not the order in which I intend to call them or the Prosecution intends to produce them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. MR. DI FAZIO: Now, the numbers 1 to 6 are the ones the Chamber has agreed can be dealt with in the normal fashion, that is, without the use of 92 bis. And the remainder, you can see from 7 to 18 are witnesses that the Chamber has indicated ought to be dealt with under the provisions of Rule 92 bis. 20 and 21 are worth -- I should mention now. Stipo Cerninski does not witness to give evidence and does not wish to attend at the -- at the Tribunal to provide evidence. I must say that that's not a matter that troubles the Prosecution, but I should point out that during the pre-trial proceedings it was the order of a differently constituted Chamber that he actually give evidence. And so the Prosecution is obliged to call him. However, I want to make it clear to this Chamber that as far as the Prosecution is concerned, it -- it has no particular reason to call him and doesn't think that he's going to advance the Prosecution's case considerably. And secondly, as I said, he doesn't want to come. I leave that matter with the Chamber, but that is the situation. We will not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- be troubled if you revoke that order and we don't have to call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Secondly, Omer Nalic, he was a gentleman I visited recently in a nearby country. I proofed him, took some instructions from him, and the Prosecution does not intend to call him. And it feels that there's not much that he can offer the Prosecution case. So there's one more witness that we do not intend to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: And then at the bottom, you can -- they speak for themselves. You know who Ewa Tabeau is and the two other witnesses concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: So the situation we face in the next two weeks or so -- or three weeks or so or possibly four weeks or so, you can see from the calendar. Next week we will be finishing with this particular witness. Ironically, the delay is going to assist the Prosecution, because I feared that what would happen was that we would start with Mr. Paradzik earlier on Tuesday and then Mr. Fitozovic would turn up on the Thursday unproofed. Somehow Mr. Paradzik would have to fill in three days, and I was worried about that. But that now looks as if that worry might be -- might not come to realisation because of the delay that we've experienced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. With the current witness. MR. DI FAZIO: But at the end of the next week -- at the end of next week, after Mr. Paradzik has finished his evidence, the Prosecution won't be in a position to offer any more witnesses to be dealt with in the usual way, because Fitozovic comes in on that day. And I've just heard to my consternation that there's some problem with that as well. He's a witness who will definitely need proofing and, and proofing for some time. He's a -- I know that he's a witness of some interest to the Defence. And then you see for the following week -- that's just my estimation of how long Mr. Fitozovic will take. And it's really an estimation that's made in ignorance, because I just don't know how long the Defence are going to be with him. Four days is just -- I must confess a figure pulled out of a hat. Without having proofed him properly, I can't tell you precisely how long his examination-in-chief will be, and I certainly can't even begin to estimate how long his cross-examination will be. But assuming it's something like the projection that I've got on this calendar, we'd start to call Subasic can the towards the end of that week, and he would go into the early part of June. If, as I hoped, Todorovic starts to give his evidence around the 10th of June -- that's what would be ideal from the Prosecution's point of view -- the 10th of June or thereabouts, there's bound to be a period of time, I would say, where we'll find ourselves unable to produce a witness to be -- to be -- well, unable to produce a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On Todorovic, the Chamber was expecting him to start on the 3rd. MR. DI FAZIO: He arrives here on the 3rd. He arrives here on the 3rd of June, I hope. I hope that he would arrive here on the 3rd of June. I would also hope that I'd have a few days to speak to him. There's already been considerable proofing of him. And because of his significance to the case, I would hope to have a few days with him at the UN Detention Centre. So it's my aim to, if possible, try and deal with him a little later, a little beyond the 3rd. Possibly earlier. But that's the sort of schedule and forecast that -- the best forecast that I could make. Now, Ms. Reidy is coming back to The Hague on the 24th of May, and she'll be coming back hopefully with some statements in proper 92 bis form. I don't believe that she's going to come back with about more than two or three statements in that time, and that may cause some surprise to the Chamber, but there's good reason for that. And let me explain to the Chamber the difficulties that face -- that she will be facing, that my colleague Mr. Weiner will be facing, in going down and taking statements. When witnesses come here, they have all the time in the world to assist the Prosecution. They -- staying in hotels. They can come into the office, and we can proof them continuously throughout the day, while other Prosecutors are in court attending -- and keeping the matter -- the business of the court proceeding in a proper fashion. When we go down to Bosnia, we're having to deal with people who are going about their ordinary lives and ordinary business, and we have to fit in with them, and it's not always possible to get mothers and fathers and elderly people to come and sit in the police station or wherever and sit there for hours and hours, as they do here, proofing and getting -- and getting instructions from them. Furthermore, once the statement is completed, it's not just a question of typing it out on the laptop computer and reading it back to the witness and then sending it here. There aren't secure fax facilities to send the statement back to -- to here. From where they're operating, the nearest secure fax facilities are in Banja Luka and Sarajevo. So it's not a question of just going down to the post office and putting the completed statement in to be brought -- to be sent here so that we can then immediately put it into the pipeline for translation. So the first statements won't get back here until the 24th of June. Then they're put in for translation. And I can't guarantee to the Chamber how long it's going to take. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You mean the 24th of May. Yes? MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry. 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: You just said 24th of June. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry. My apologies. 24th of May. In the best of worlds, it will be translated within a day or two or three. That's in the best of worlds. And I fear that reality is that it will take somewhat longer for the that for them to be officially translated. Then we get to the point where we can serve them on the Defence and the two or three-week period starts. So there's every possibility that by about the middle of June, they'll only just be starting to come through, the 92 bis statements. And I'm concerned that if we're held rigidly to this -- to this order of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Not really. Because the Trial Chamber is trying to look at how best it will deal with the rest of the witnesses. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes. I -- let me state again that the Prosecution is -- has no quarrel with the Chamber on that and the Prosecution is doing whatever it can to adopt that procedure and the Prosecution hopes that a good number - a good number - of those witnesses that the Chamber wishes us to deal with under -- under 92 bis will be dealt with pursuant to that rule. I'm not trying to undermine that in the slightest. But I do want, if the Prosecution is -- if the Chamber is so minded, to have a bit more flexibility, to be able to pick and choose some of the witnesses from that 92 bis list and bring them here orally while we're waiting for these processes to be dealt with and handled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Yes, definitely. That -- instead of the Chamber adjourning. MR. DI FAZIO: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, that's what I wanted to -- that's the appeal that I wanted to make to the Chamber. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As long as we complete these others, like number 22, number 23. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I had hoped to fit in -- use Ewa Tabeau next week, but she's in fact on a mission in -- in Bosnia. So can I say this to the Chamber: Can you please provide us with flexibility and allow us to call some of the witnesses who are currently 92 bis witnesses in the usual fashion until the statements come -- start coming through the pipeline, until all of those processes have been properly attended to and we can just bring them in and deal with them in the way that the Chamber wants us to under that rule. And if we do that, I think we can keep proceeding with live witnesses until we get to this -- the point where they start being dealt with under the provisions of Rule 92 bis. For example, number 13 lives in a nearby country, and he would be an excellent witness to bring in at short notice and to plug in any gaps that might arise. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because there's also the videolink witnesses, isn't there? MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes. Yes, there's -- yes. There's that witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because we can also go ahead with that. MR. DI FAZIO: We could -- we could do that, yes. But my main concern is this: We haven't lost sight of what you want us to do, and we're fully on board with that and will do whatever we can to put the witnesses into the right form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. The Trial Chamber's concern is there must be a flow of witnesses. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The second one is as much as possible, let's get Rule 92 worked out, because it will enable us to -- perhaps even to complete three, four, five witnesses per week. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If that were to be done. Because the greater part of the sitting hours will be used by cross-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that fully, and as I said we've started it already. Ms. Reidy is down there and Mr. Weiner's turn will come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. And -- MR. DI FAZIO: As may mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: But at this stage, I'd just like that extra flexibility. And if we have that flexibility, I can assure the Chamber that we can keep the witnesses coming one after the other. Whether they be dealt with in the normal fashion or under 92 bis, but we'll keep up that flow of witnesses. And the point will be reached eventually, I should think, where most of the remainder of the witnesses will be -- will be 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Has the Prosecution got the Trial Chamber's order yet on Todorovic? MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because -- MR. DI FAZIO: Nothing has come across my desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see. Because the Trial Chamber's position is that he should start giving evidence on the 3rd of June. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Now, in view of the problem we are having with the current witness, depending on whether or not on Tuesday she will be able to continue, maybe -- we may look at the calendar again. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'll do that. If Your Honours please, would the Chamber be inconvenienced if he did arrive on the 3rd and if the Chamber were able to usefully occupy its time for a few days with another witness and I could then bring him on sometime after the 3rd, because it's my earnest desire to speak to him again before I bring him into court. I've already spent a lot of time proofing him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. The Trial Chamber was hoping that he would be brought in before the 3rd. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, that would suit me as well. As long as I've got that opportunity to speak to him before he starts his evidence. That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because the Chamber is expecting since we are starting in the morning at 9.00, he should be in the witness box, in which case he'll be brought in much earlier than the 3rd. MR. DI FAZIO: I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: That would -- that can be done. That can be engineered or brought about. I understand from having spoken to Registry people that he was to be brought in on the 3rd or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh. Anyway that one -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think that one will be sorted out depending on our situation on Tuesday with the current witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps that can be finalised then. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, as far as the Prosecution is concerned it really doesn't matter whether he starts on the 3rd or whether he starts on the 10th. What does matter to the Prosecution is that we be given an opportunity to speak to him for one or two days beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: That's our main concern, because there are still a number of issues that we have to deal with him notwithstanding all the time that we have spent with him. So can I, Your Honours, assume that I am permitted to call some of these witnesses who were intended to be 92 bis witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: As long as they are called after all these others who are still waiting to be called. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes. Of course. We'll deal with -- yes. If things -- if I'm completely wrong and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Things move much faster. MR. DI FAZIO: If things move much faster, then of course that would happen. I have no desire to abandon this general game plan. But all -- as I said, can I assume that if things don't go in -- ideally, that I can continue to call live witnesses until the 92 bis statements start to flow through?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. If we have reached the stage when they're finished. On the witness, on number 20, Stipo Cerninski, the Trial Chamber will look at what the summary says before it can decide whether or not he should actually be called at the instance of the Trial Chamber. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any matters from the Defence? No. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one comment in principle, which will probably be a repetition. But I have reason to repeat it on the occasion of this last testimony. You have probably noticed that the past few witnesses whom we heard had given earlier statements -- or I should use the word "interviews" -- and were notified to us as accompanied by so-called informal interviews or notes of the Prosecutor. We received notes of interviews which were conducted just before their testimony, and that was the only thing that we had to help us in relation to some facts which had not been mentioned previously. However, in the case of this witness, we received absolutely nothing from the Office of the Prosecutor, and we heard a lot of completely new things which were not covered by any of the previous notes or interviews, and therefore I would be very grateful that if the Prosecution office does conduct certain interviews, especially if the accused are specifically mentioned and if it was the stand of this Trial Chamber from the beginning that we should avoid games of hide and seek, if such interviews are conducted, as I said, I hope we can get the notes. Otherwise, we are prevented from conducting appropriate consultations with our clients before the testimony. And I repeat: I am saying this because we have heard from this witness a large number of things that had not been mentioned and we have only the statements which are even unsigned by the witnesses in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to respond to that, because I'm the one who usually provides the -- the summaries. This witness came on a last-minute basis on Sunday, so I had to try and proof her very quickly. When I received some information -- because she does talk about extensive information in her statement. And when she provided more detail and it looked like suddenly she was going on the witness stand on Monday, what I did was -- and I told I would follow up with a report -- number one, I contacted each Defence counsel personally to tell them exactly what in relation to their client she was going to provide. I contacted Mr. Lukic first. He contacted Mr. Lazarevic to have Mr. Lazarevic call me because I could not get hold of Mr. Lazarevic. Then I personally contacted Mr. Pantelic to let each one of them know what exactly they were going to testify to. Yesterday at lunchtime I tried to type it out. I had trouble with the computer. Everything is in the computer, I can't take it out. It's in a laptop computer. I'll be happy to provide it either today if we can get it out or I'll retype it myself tomorrow morning. But I didn't want to Court to think that no discovery as to further specifics of what she had provided in her report were provided, that they were reported orally as opposed to in writing. If I can't get that out of the laptop computer, which I'm having trouble doing, I'll just retype it tomorrow morning and I'll give it to each -- or I'll retype it tonight. And if they'll stay around for about 30 minutes, I'll provide it tonight. I'm a slow typist, and it's one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution should do that as soon as possible so that the Defence counsels can properly consult with their clients for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. They can have it tonight within 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to avoid any unclarity. It's true that Mr. Weiner called me on the phone, but it was only to say that he had nothing new concerning my client. So if there is anything new, as he says now, I will be grateful for the notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. The Trial Chamber can only trust the Prosecution to do their duty accordingly for continuation of these proceedings according to the rules. We shall adjourn now and the proceedings will continue on Tuesday at 14.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
